title: Membrane: A Self-Evolving Contrastive Safety Memory for LLM Agent Defense

object.carrier: Contrastive Safety Memory (CSM): an external writable cell store where each cell m=(P, D, T) pairs an Attack Profile P (attack strategy, requested action, harm objective - mechanism-level fields indexed by strategy, not surface topic) with contrastive Decision Criteria D=(d_unsafe, d_safe) and an optional Tool-Action Context T for agent settings; the store evolves via a Memory Planner (create/update/delete/skip), a Memory Writer that synthesizes cell content, and a non-LLM validator enforcing schema, duplicate, and capacity constraints; inference retrieves candidate cells (vector retrieval) filtered by a Retrieval Critic before the Guard decides

safety_property.statement: A precise safety boundary under evolving jailbreaks: harmful queries must be blocked (low ASR) while superficially similar benign queries must be admitted (low FRR), with the writable memory itself resistant to poisoning (safe-as-unsafe injection that induces over-refusal, and unsafe-as-safe injection that induces jailbreaks). Failure conditions: jailbroken (guard permits the harmful side), over-refusal (guard rejects the benign side), or poisoned cells steering decisions.
safety_property.operationalized_as: ASR (fraction of harmful prompts answered / harmful tasks not refused), FRR (fraction of benign prompts refused), and F1 = 2(1-ASR)(1-FRR)/((1-ASR)+(1-FRR)) on HarmBench (320 harmful prompts paired with 320 in-house benign counterparts per transformed setting; 7 evaluation conditions incl. untransformed) and AgentHarm (176 harmful + 176 benign), with warmup N=80 (HarmBench) / N=32 (AgentHarm) bootstrapped then frozen; memory-poisoning robustness (ASR/FRR at 10% and 20% writer-mediated injection rates, top-k retrieval rate of poisoned cells, critic filter rate); per-query latency (mean/p95 seconds).

capabilities: Jailbreak attackers across six modern mechanisms: iterative refinement (PAIR), persuasion-based rephrasing (PAP), tree-of-thought search (TAP), nested instruction rewriting (ReNeLLM), character-level perturbation (FlipAttack), and lifelong strategy exploration (AutoDAN-Turbo)

Memory poisoner injects cells through the normal write path at rates rho of 10% and 20%, via two strategies: safe-as-unsafe (manipulate memory into refusing benign queries) and unsafe-as-safe (force acceptance of harmful queries), with the standard guard mechanism suppressed during the attack
assumptions: Attacker and scorer are the same fixed model (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct) across all defenses, so cross-method differences come from the defense rather than the attack data

Bootstrapped memory is frozen during evaluation (static inference pipeline), isolating guard behavior from on-the-fly memory composition and keeping comparisons against static and fine-tuned baselines fair
not_covered: Fully adaptive white-box adversaries with access to the guard, the memory store, and the deployment pipeline are explicitly not modeled (the authors note this setting requires access-control and monitoring mechanisms beyond the algorithmic guard)
Cross-lingual, multimodal, and nested-agent deployments are out of scope (text-only English benchmarks)
The protected model is fixed to Qwen3-8B in the main tables (Appendix G sweeps sizes/backbones)

intervention.name: Membrane: self-evolving guardrail on Contrastive Safety Memory with Paired Self-Evolution
intervention.description: An external guard that decides safe/unsafe before the target model or tool-using agent acts. Paired Self-Evolution: each interaction pairs a harmful prompt with a benign counterpart exercising the same surface mechanism; the verdict (jailbroken / over-refusal / correct) plus the paired queries form an evolution signal from which one contrastive cell is written (create, update, delete, or skip), so every update commits a contrastive boundary rather than a one-sided exemplar; a deterministic non-LLM validator rejects writes violating schema/duplicate/capacity constraints. Inference: vector retrieval of candidate cells, a Retrieval Critic filters inapplicable matches, and the Guard issues the decision grounded on kept cells. Membrane lite disables the Retrieval Critic for lower latency.

controls.name: Prompt-level guards: Self-Reminder, SmoothLLM, SelfDefend, TrustAgent, ShieldAgent
Memory-augmented adaptive guards: RAD, GuardAgent, AGrail
Ablations: -CSM decision criteria, -Paired Self-Evolution, -Retrieval Critic, -Tool-Action Context (Table 3)

results.claim: Membrane achieves the highest F1 on all six jailbreak attacks across both benchmarks; on HarmBench it drives ReNeLLM ASR to 0.3% (vs 11.3% for RAD, the best baseline) and completely suppresses FlipAttack at 0.0% ASR (vs 7.8% best baseline).
results.metric: ASR (%) per attack on HarmBench, lower is better
results.comparison: best baselines: RAD 11.3% (ReNeLLM), 7.8% (FlipAttack), 25.0% (TAP), 21.3% (PAIR); FRR held to 2.9%-6.1%
results.setting: HarmBench, 320 harmful prompts + 320 benign counterparts per transformed setting, Qwen3-8B target, warmup N=80 frozen (Table 1)
results.quote: On ReNeLLM, Membrane achieves an ASR of 0.3%, vastly outperforming the 11.3% achieved by RAD.

denominator.how_counted: ASR = fraction of the 320 harmful prompts answered per transformed setting; FRR = fraction of the 320 benign counterparts refused

results.claim: Cost reading (over-refusal): on AgentHarm, Membrane keeps benign refusal (FRR) at 7-14% across all settings, substantially below memory-augmented baselines GuardAgent (52-53%) and AGrail (27-32%) and prompt-level TrustAgent (73-85%).
results.metric: False Refusal Rate (FRR, %) on AgentHarm benign tasks
results.comparison: GuardAgent 52-53%; AGrail 27-32%; TrustAgent 73-85%; static guards reach 73-85%
results.setting: AgentHarm, 176 benign counterparts, Qwen3-8B agent, warmup N=32 frozen (Table 2)
results.quote: While effectively blocking these attacks, Membrane consistently restricts the FRR to a range of 7% to 14% across all settings.

denominator.how_counted: FRR = refusal rate over the 176 benign AgentHarm tasks per attack setting

results.claim: On AgentHarm, Membrane cuts FlipAttack ASR to 0.9% versus 100% for the unguarded agent, and reaches F1 89.2% (ReNeLLM) and 93.0% (FlipAttack) - the highest across all attack methods with a large margin on text-transformation attacks.
results.quote: Membrane drastically reduces the ASR compared to the unprotected agent, achieving an ASR of 0.9% on FlipAttack versus 100% for the vanilla baseline.

denominator.how_counted: ASR = fraction of the 176 harmful tasks not refused, per attack setting

results.claim: Cross-attack transfer: cells warmed on one jailbreak method retain 87-88% of the same-attack F1 when evaluated against other attacks sharing the underlying strategy (model safety 80.8% vs 92.6%; agent safety 69.5% vs 79.2%).
results.metric: cross-attack F1 retention (% of same-attack F1)
results.setting: For each attack A, CSM warmed only on A then evaluated frozen against the other attacks (Figure 3, full matrices in Appendix I)
results.quote: the transfer F1 retains 87%87\% of the same attack F1 in model safety (80.8%80.8\% vs. 92.6%92.6\%) and 88%88\% in agent safety (69.5%69.5\% vs. 79.2%79.2\%).

denominator.how_counted: Matrix means over off-diagonal attack pairs; model safety over 320-prompt HarmBench settings, agent safety over 176-task AgentHarm settings

results.claim: Poisoning robustness: even at a 20% writer-mediated injection rate, defensive performance stays near the clean baseline - unsafe-as-safe raises ASR only from 2.1% to 2.5% and safe-as-unsafe raises FRR from 10.8% to 15.4%, because poisoned-cell retrieval rates stay at 2.3-7.5% and the Retrieval Critic eliminates 33-40% of surfaced poisoned cells.
results.metric: ASR / FRR (%) under 10% and 20% poisoning; retrieval rate Ret; critic filter rate
results.comparison: clean baseline ASR 2.1% / FRR 5.0-10.8% depending on branch
results.setting: HarmBench, 80-event clean warmup then 10%/20% injection, standard guard suppressed during attack (Table 4)
results.quote: Even under the 20% injection rate, the defensive performance remains nearly identical to the clean baseline.

denominator.how_counted: ASR/FRR over the HarmBench harmful/benign evaluation pairs after warmup; poison rate rho = fraction of injected writes; Ret = share of poisoned cells in top-k retrievals; Critic = share of surfaced poisoned cells filtered

results.claim: Cost reading (latency): full Membrane runs at 12.89 s (HarmBench) and 14.59 s (AgentHarm) mean per query - far faster than SmoothLLM (156.93 s) and AGrail (25.22 s) - while Membrane lite (no Retrieval Critic) runs at 2.33/2.43 s with F1 91.7%/78.6%, still beating every baseline regardless of latency tier.
results.metric: per-query defense latency (mean seconds, single-stream) with F1
results.comparison: SmoothLLM 156.93 s @ F1 21.3; RAD 6.31 s @ 77.1; SelfDefend 0.90 s @ 59.6; AGrail 25.22 s @ 64.2; GuardAgent 5.94 s @ 59.6 (Table 5)
results.setting: Single-stream per-query overhead averaged over the seven evaluation settings, HarmBench and AgentHarm (Table 5)
results.quote: The full Membrane successfully maintains the highest F1 scores while operating significantly faster than computationally heavy baselines such as SmoothLLM (156.93 seconds) and AGrail (25.22 seconds).

denominator.how_counted: Mean and p95 per-query latency in seconds over the evaluation queries of the seven settings; query counts follow the per-setting HarmBench/AgentHarm splits

results.claim: Ablation: removing Paired Self-Evolution causes the largest F1 drop (-7.4 points HarmBench, -11.5 points AgentHarm), and removing the decision criteria or Tool-Action Context raises AgentHarm FRR from 6.3% to 20.5% and 17.1% - the contrastive structure is what suppresses over-refusal.
results.metric: F1 (%) and FRR (%) per ablated component, averaged over seven settings
results.value: F1 93.4 -> 86.0 (w/o Paired Self-Evolution, HarmBench); FRR 6.3 -> 20.5% (w/o decision criteria, AgentHarm)
results.setting: Component ablations averaged over the seven evaluation settings (Table 3)
results.quote: Removing Paired Self-Evolution causes the most severe performance degradation, decreasing the F1 score by 7.4% and 11.5% points on HarmBench and AgentHarm, respectively.

denominator.how_counted: Averages over the seven evaluation settings (six attacks + untransformed) on each benchmark

limitations.statement: Evaluation is text-only English on HarmBench/AgentHarm; cross-lingual, multimodal, and nested-agent deployments need separate benchmarks and threat models.
limitations.quote: Membrane is evaluated on text-only English model-safety and agent-safety benchmarks. This follows the coverage of HarmBench and AgentHarm and keeps comparisons to existing guardrails controlled; cross-lingual, multimodal, and nested-agent deployments require separate benchmark construction and threat models, which we leave to future work.

limitations.statement: The main tables fix the protected model to Qwen3-8B to avoid conflating guard behavior with target-model scale; robustness to this choice is only partially addressed by the Appendix G sweeps.
limitations.quote: Our main tables fix the protected model to Qwen3-8B to avoid conflating guard behavior with target-model scale or backbone effects.

limitations.statement: Fully adaptive white-box adversaries with access to the guard, memory store, and deployment pipeline are not modeled and would require access-control and monitoring beyond the algorithmic guard.
limitations.quote: The remaining attacks we do not model are fully adaptive white-box adversaries with access to the guard, memory store, and deployment pipeline. This operational setting requires access-control and monitoring mechanisms beyond the algorithmic guard studied here.

limitations.statement: All response-level evaluation is delegated to a single judge (Gemini 3 Flash), applied to every defense so residual judge bias is shared across baselines.
limitations.quote: All response-level evaluation is delegated to Gemini 3 Flash, a model family distinct from the Qwen3-8B guard, to reduce correlated blind spots between the guard and the judge. The same judge is applied to every defense, so any residual judge bias is shared across baselines.

reproduction.data: HarmBench (320 harmful + 320 in-house benign counterparts per transformed setting), AgentHarm (176 + 176), six attack suites (PAIR, PAP, TAP, ReNeLLM, FlipAttack, AutoDAN-Turbo) constructed with Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct as attacker and scorer; Appendices F/G/H/I document construction, sweeps, and full per-attack results; Appendix J lists artifact licenses
